adf_holm.scope: ADF correction across unique computed series/transformation/regression tests only; no request-row replication and no adjusted joint ADF/KPSS classification.

readout_conclusion: Log returns fit the nominal stationarity pattern more often than log price levels on these selected segments. Of 318 testable log-return paths, 304 were stationarity compatible and 14 produced conflicting rejections. Their ADF unit-root null was rejected after global Holm correction in 318 cases. Neither clock supplied a 300-point contiguous price run at the primary 250-ms freshness setting; the tested evidence comes from longer-age sensitivities. The 318 testable paths share market and event contexts and are not 318 independent experiments. No transformation is applied automatically, and the native level-based latency matcher remains unchanged.
interpretation: Exploratory segment-specific diagnostics; nominal classifications are not a transformation rule or causal event-class comparison.
limitations: The original latency/event study is unchanged; this diagnostic does not test irregular latency observations or automatically transform main-study inputs.

Within each planned one-second price window, select the longest strict no-gap supported run using quality alone; ties use the earliest run. Invalid intervals are not interpolated or stitched together.

Three hundred one-second observations are approximately five minutes (299 seconds between endpoints); 600 observations are approximately ten minutes. The 600-point flag is descriptive, not validation of long-span stationarity.
Log-level c and log-return c are separate diagnostics. The log-level ct specification is a deterministic-trend sensitivity, paired with ct in both ADF and KPSS.
Nominal joint classifications use opposite null hypotheses at the stated alpha; failing to reject is not proof of a null hypothesis.
ADF Holm adjustment uses unique computed tests only. It does not convert the displayed nominal ADF/KPSS matrix into a jointly adjusted classification.
KPSS p-values are table-bounded near 0.01 and 0.10; preserve bound relations and warnings rather than interpreting endpoints as precise probabilities.
A large number of one-second samples does not replace a long time span. Event-related breaks and market microstructure can affect test behavior.
The longest supported segment can represent only a fraction of a scheduled window; conclusions concern that selected segment, not the whole session.
Requests, identical price paths and related event bundles are dependent; grouped classifications do not establish event-type causal effects or independent replication counts.
Stationarity diagnostics alone do not select a model transformation. Differencing a price path can change the native first-passage price-target estimand.
Exploratory diagnostics added after inspecting the latency study, not a preregistered event-effect test.
An eligible subwindow is not proof that the complete thirty-minute window is observable or stationary.
Five minutes is the minimum tested span; ten-minute runs are flagged descriptively, not a statistical power guarantee.
Dense sampling does not replace a long time span; short intraday windows limit unit-root inference.
Pre/post splitting avoids pooling the scheduled event boundary but cannot remove other structural breaks.
Per-venue stationarity support is not joint common-venue support for a VAR or cointegration model.
Irregular and censored latency observations are not subjected to regular-time ADF/KPSS tests.
Neither a nominal test classification nor differencing repairs missing books, ambiguous records or clock differences.
No transformation is applied to the audited latency study and no event-level causal effect is estimated here.
